note: 29 expert reviewers over 445 benchmarks find safety and robustness claims routinely lack construct validity, with eight fixes.
title: Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks
explain_beginner: When a company says its AI model scored well on a "safety" or "reasoning" test, how do we know that test actually measured safety or reasoning, rather than something else, like memorized text or a narrow trick? This paper asks whether the tests the AI field uses to measure abstract qualities in language models actually measure what they claim to, a property researchers call construct validity, borrowed from decades of work in psychological testing. A team of 29 expert reviewers examined 445 published AI benchmarks from major research conferences, checking how carefully each one defined what it was testing, turned that definition into concrete questions, and scored the answers. They found widespread problems: many benchmarks tackle concepts nobody agrees on a clear definition for, most never run basic statistical checks on score differences between models, and most rely on artificial questions rather than realistic ones. Based on this, the authors offer eight practical recommendations for anyone building a benchmark, aimed at making the resulting scores trustworthy.
explain_business: This paper is a warning label for anyone making purchasing or deployment decisions based on a vendor's benchmark scores. It finds that across hundreds of peer-reviewed AI benchmarks, most do not run the statistical tests needed to know whether a score difference between two models is real or noise, many test made-up scenarios instead of realistic use cases, and terms like safety or robustness are often used without an agreed definition behind the number. For a business evaluating AI vendors, a benchmark score alone, even from a reputable source, is not sufficient evidence that a model is safe, robust, or good at reasoning for your specific use case. The practical implication is to ask vendors what phenomenon a benchmark claims to measure, whether the task resembles your actual use case, and whether reported differences between models were statistically tested. This paper does not evaluate any specific commercial AI product, but it supplies a checklist, the eight recommendations, for interrogating a vendor's evaluation claims before relying on them.
explain_practitioner: This is a systematic review, not a new benchmark. The authors define construct validity as the degree to which a benchmark score supports a specific claim about a phenomenon, and split each benchmark into four parts: the abstract phenomenon targeted, the concrete task, the scoring metric, and the claims drawn from results. Twenty-nine expert reviewers coded 445 benchmarks from ICML, ICLR, NeurIPS, ACL, NAACL, and EMNLP from 2018 to 2024. Key findings: only 53.4 percent of papers explicitly discuss construct validity, 47.8 percent target contested phenomena without a consensus definition, only 16 percent use statistical significance testing between models, 27 percent rely on convenience sampling, and 40.7 percent use constructed rather than real-world tasks. The eight recommendations cover precise definitions, controlling confounds, representative sampling, documenting dataset reuse, contamination checks, statistical testing, error analysis, and justifying real-world relevance. The authors' own limitations: the review covers only peer-reviewed conference benchmarks, excluding industry ones, and an automated filtering step, despite 84 percent validation accuracy, may have missed some relevant papers.
